 SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Trump Visits Arlington Cemetery as His Proposed Arch Faces Growing Opposition
 An expanding legal fight over the proposed site of President Trump’s 250-foot triumphal arch looms over his visit to Arlington National Cemetery on Veterans Day.
 Listen · 8:14 min Share full article 
 A view along Memorial Bridge toward Arlington Cemetery, which would be blocked by Mr. Trump’s planned arch. Credit... Eric Lee for The New York Times By Zach Montague 
 Reporting from Washington
 Nov. 11, 2026 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. Encuentra más de nuestra cobertura en los resultados de búsqueda. Add The New York Times as a preferred source on Google Agrega The New York Times como fuente preferida en Google › 
 President Trump traveled to Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday to lay a wreath in honor of fallen service members, a time-honored presidential tradition on Veterans Day at a site that could be dramatically reshaped by his proposal to build a 250-foot triumphal arch in a traffic circle just outside the cemetery’s main entrance.
 Mr. Trump’s arch project is being challenged in court by a trio of Vietnam War veterans ; Arlington County, Va.; the state of Virginia; the District of Columbia ; and as of Tuesday, members of the Kennedy family , whose relatives’ graves sit at the emotional heart of the cemetery.
 A common thread throughout the suits is the contention that the giant arch, which would loom over the nearly 640-acre military cemetery in Virginia, would have a negative effect on it.
 How Trump’s Proposed Arch Would Change D.C.
 The Times created a 3-D model of the 250-foot monument to show how it would affect a symbolic sightline.
 The planned site of the arch holds “symbolic significance as the physical and ceremonial connection between Washington, D.C. and Arlington National Cemetery — the final resting place of more than 400,000 active-duty service members, veterans, and their family members,” Virginia and the District of Columbia contended in their joint lawsuit.
 “For more than a century, that direct sight line has stood as a testament to the reunification of the nation after the Civil War and a point of reflection for visitors,” Arlington County said in a legal filing.
